CHAPTER 13

## Orthopedic Disorders

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Orthopedic conditions
- $ Arthritis
- Osteoarthritis
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- $ Fibromyalgia
- Orthopedic injuries
- $ Shoulder: rotator cuff, impingement syndrome
- $ Elbow: tennis elbow
- $ Wrist: scaphoid fracture
- $ Low back pain
- $ Hip pain
- $ Knee: ACL, meniscal injuries
- $ Ankle/foot: ankle sprain, plantar fasciitis, Morton neuroma

## NOTES Arthritic Joints

## Osteoarthritis

- Joint pain: exacerbated by use
- Stiffness: morning, ≤60 min
- $ Can affect any joint
- May be unilateral or bilateral
- Knees, hips, spine and hands
- $ Limited range of motion
- $ Joint tenderness
- $ Crepitus
- $ Joint effusion possible
- $ Bony remodeling

## Diagnosis of Osteoarthritis

Clinical diagnosis

- Joint pain (single/few)
- Age ≥45 years
- Morning stiffness (≤60 min)

Radiograph supportive if:

- Presence of joint space narrowing and/or osteophyte radiograph

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

## Osteoarthritis of Hands

TIP: Bouchard are BELOW Heberden Heberden are HIGHER than Bouchard

<!-- image -->

## Treatment of Osteoarthritis

Nonpharmacologic measures first!

- Patient education
- Exercise: aerobic and strengthening
- Weight loss if appropriate
- Heat, cold, ultrasound, acupuncture: may be effective in some cases

## QUESTION #1

What is the first-line pharmacologic management of osteoarthritis?

1. Acetaminophen
2. NSAIDs
3. Opioids
4. Duloxetine

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #2

A patient who has osteoarthritis asks if it is safe to take meloxicam daily for their pain. This medication may be unsafe if the patient has which of the following conditions?

1. Heart failure
2. Depression
3. Hypothyroidism
4. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Pharmacologic Management

ONLY as needed!

| Medication                         | Characteristics                        |
|------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| NSAIDs                             | First-line: topical then oral          |
| Acetaminophen                      | No benefit/safety concerns             |
| Topical capsaicin                  | May be helpful                         |
| Duloxetine                         | Alternative: if NSAIDs contraindicated |
| Injectable steroids                | Very short duration                    |
| Glucosamine, chondroitin, fish oil | Lack of evidence                       |
| Opioids                            | Avoid! Risks outweigh benefits         |

## Rheumatoid Arthritis

- Autoimmune disease
- Symmetrical, peripheral polyarthritis
- Leads to joint deformity and destruction
- Morning stiffness lasts >60 min

TIP: RA and OA both affect the hands. Understand the differences!

## Rheumatoid Workup

Anti-CCP antibodies: citrullinated peptides/proteins

Higher specificity than RF, similar sensitivity to RF

Rheumatoid factor (RF) Acute phase reactants: ESR, CRP

ANA: negative may exclude SLE

CBC, LFTs, BUN, Cr, uric acid level, UA

## QUESTION #3

Which of the following is a false statement about fibromyalgia?

1. It is an inflammatory condition.
2. It causes tenderness to soft tissues.
3. It typically occurs between the ages of 20 and 55 years.
4. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

## Fibromyalgia Assessment

Widespread pain index

- 19 painful body regions
- 1 pt/region, max score 19

Symptom severity score (Scale 0-3, max score 12)

1. Degree of fatigue
2. Waking unrefreshed
3. # of cognitive symptoms ("fibro fog")
4. # of somatic symptoms (abd cramping, IBS symptoms, headache, depression, etc.)

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Fibromyalgia: Diagnosis

- ACR preliminary diagnostic criteria (2016)

<!-- image -->

WPI = Widespread Pain Index

- SS = Symptom Severity (SS) Scale

## NOTES

## NOTES Fibromyalgia: Initial Management

- Patient education
- Sleep hygiene
- Treat comorbidities: mood, sleep disorders
- Exercise: aerobic conditioning, stretching, strengthening
- Medication for pain: amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregabalin, others

A patient has started a new job as a painter and after 6 weeks of work, they report pain in the lateral deltoid when raising their arm overhead. A positive empty can test is elicited by the NP. Which of the following is suspected?

## Specific Tests for Rotator Cuff

| Test                                                     | Movement                                                                                             | Positive Finding                                                                                                                                         |
|----------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Neer test [passive painful arc maneuver] (supraspinatus) | Abduction to 180° (raising arm overhead)                                                             | Pain with impingement: · 90°: Mild · 60°-70°: Moderate · 45°: Severe                                                                                     |
| Active painful arc (supraspinatus)                       | Examiner raises patient arm overhead, while exerting pressure to prevent shrug                       | Pain beyond 90°                                                                                                                                          |
| Hawkins-Kennedy test                                     | Flexion with internal rotation                                                                       | Pain elicited by internal rotation                                                                                                                       |
| Jobe's (empty can) test (supraspinatus)                  | Straight arm, 90° abduction, 30° of forward flexion, internal rotation; adduction against resistance | Weakness with or without pain                                                                                                                            |
| Drop arm test (supraspinatus)                            | Patient passively lowers arm from a fully abducted position                                          | Positive if unable to lower the affected arm with smooth, coordinated movement compared to unaffected arm. A sudden drop with pain = full thickness tear |
| External rotation test (infraspinatus)                   | Hold shoulder in adduction, elbow bent 90°                                                           | Weakness with external rotation against resistance                                                                                                       |

## Lateral Epicondylitis

Inflammation of the extensor tendons (posterior forearm) where they attach to lateral epicondyle

Occurs from repetitive motion of the extensor muscles of the forearm

## Scaphoid Fracture

| Imaging        | · Radiograph/PA/Lat/Oblique/Scaphoid Wrist · If negative, get MRI or CT · If MRI unavailable, repeat radiography in 7-14 days   |
|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Immobilize     | · Suspected Fx, not confirmed by radiography · Confirmed Fx, via radiography or MRI $ Immobilization up to 5 months!            |

TIP: Initial imaging can be falsely negative. When suspicious: immobilize, repeat the imaging, & refer

## Low Back Pain: Differential Diagnosis

| Spinal                                   | Extraspinal (Visceral)   | Nonmechanical Spinal Disease                                                                                                                    |
|------------------------------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| · Lumbar strain/ · musculoskeletal (85%) | · Prostatitis            | · Neoplasia (metastasis) · Infection (osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) · Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis) |
| · Degenerative disk (10%) · Spondylosis  | · Endometriosis          | · Neoplasia (metastasis) · Infection (osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) · Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis) |
| · Herniated disk (4%)                    | · Nephrolithiasis        | · Neoplasia (metastasis) · Infection (osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) · Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis) |
| · Osteoporotic fracture (4%)             | · Aortic aneurysm        | · Neoplasia (metastasis) · Infection (osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) · Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis) |
| · Spinal stenosis                        | · Pancreatitis           | · Neoplasia (metastasis) · Infection (osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) · Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis) |
| · Kyphosis/scoliosis                     | · Penetrating ulcer      | · Neoplasia (metastasis) · Infection (osteomyelitis, epidural abscess) · Inflammatory arthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic spondylitis) |

## Low Back Pain: Physical Examination

- Inspection/palpation/percussion of spine
- Gait-heal-to-toe walk
- Neurologic examination: motor, sensory, reflexes
- Assess for radiculopathy
- $ Straight leg raise (SLR):
- Examiner raises patient's extended leg with the ankle dorsiflexed.
- Positive if sciatica is reproduced between 10° and 60° in the affected leg

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Low Back Pain: Imaging

| Indications      | · Pain lasting >4 weeks · Unresponsive to conservative treatment                                                                                                                                       |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| MRI is preferred | · For most conditions · May have to get radiography first                                                                                                                                              |
| Emergent imaging | · Neurologic deficits (e.g., extremity weakness loss of DTR, sensory deficit, bowel/bladder incontinence · Suspicion of neoplasm (e.g., metastasis) · Infection: fever, IV drug use, immunocompromised |

## Low Back Pain: Management

- Nonpharmacologic management
- $ Heat
- $ Physical therapy
- $ Massage
- Pharm management
- $ NSAID (systemic)
- $ +/- Muscle relaxants

1. Numbness radiates down his posterior leg.
2. The pain is worse with movement.
3. Numbness of buttocks and perineum.
4. The pain is colicky and radiates to the flank.

## Cauda Equina Syndrome

- Marked neurologic disability
- Saddle anesthesia
- Etiology
- $ Neural tube defects
- $ Infection
- $ Inflammation
- $ Mass
- $ Lumbar spinal stenosis
- $ Injury
- $ Herniated disc

<!-- image -->

## Expected Course

90% of cases of low back pain have resolution of symptoms within 4-6 weeks.

## NOTES Hip Pain

Character, location, and pattern of pain give clues to diagnosis

## Hip Pain Characteristics

| Pain Characteristics                    | Differential Diagnosis               |
|-----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Lateral, aggravated by direct pressure  | Trochanteric bursitis                |

| Constant pain, especially at night time | Infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic |
| Anterior hip/groin pain                 | Hip joint: OA                        |
| Posterior hip pain                      | SI joint, LBP                        |

## NOTES Assessment of Knee Pain: Tests

|               | Test               | Method                                                                                                                             | Identifies                                              |
|---------------|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| Meniscal tear | McMurray test      | Passive flexion and extension of the knee, then repeat with the tibia internally and externally rotated                            | Popping, pain at joint line, or limited range of motion |
|               | Apley test         | Knee flexed to 90°, stabilize thigh, press heel directly downward while internally and externally rotating foot                    | Pain or pop                                             |
| MCL injury    | Valgus stress test | Slight hip flexion and abduction, knee flexed, exert gentle valgus (inward) stress with hands over lateral knee and proximal tibia | Laxity of 30° flexion suggestive of MCL injury          |
| LCL           | Varus stress test  | Slight hip flexion and abduction, knee flexed, exert gentle varus (outward) stress with hands over lateral knee and proximal tibia | Laxity of 30° flexion suggestive of LCL injury          |

## Assessment of Knee Pain: Tests

|     | Test             | Method                                                                               | Identifies                                                                            |
|-----|------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ACL | Lachman test     | Most sensitive; flex knee to 20°-30°, translate tibia with anteriorly directed force | Soft or mushy end feel                                                                |
| ACL | Anterior drawer  | Flex knee to 90°, translate tibia with anteriorly directed force                     | Lack of end feel or excessive anterior translation relative to the contralateral side |
| PCL | Posterior drawer | Flex knee to 90°, posteriorly directed force to the tibia                            | Lack of end feel or excessive posterior translation                                   |

## QUESTION #8

An adult patient presents with right ankle pain following an injury that occurred earlier this morning. According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, a radiograph is indicated if the patient:

1. is unable to bear weight for 10 steps.
2. has tenderness only in the malleolar zone.
3. has generalized ankle tenderness.
4. was able to bear weight immediately after the injury.

<!-- image -->

## Ottawa Ankle Rules

<!-- image -->

| X-ray if:                                                                                               | X-ray of ankle                                                             | X-ray of foot                                                                                 |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| X-ray if: · Unable to bear · Unable to bear weight immediately following injury or four steps in office | X-ray of ankle · Bony tenderness · · Bony tenderness in the malleolar zone | X-ray of foot Bony tenderness · Bony tenderness in the midfoot (navicular or base of 5th MTP) |

weight immediately

following injury or

four steps in office

## Ankle Sprain

Stretching or partial tearing of the lateral or deltoid ligaments of the ankle

Lateral: most common; inversion of plantarflexed foot

Medial: rare eversion injury, strongest of ankle ligaments

## Grade 2 sprain

- Most common sprain seen in primary care office
- Presents with some joint instability, restricted range of motion, ambulation painful

in the malleolar

zone in the midfoot

(navicular or base

of 5th MTP)

<!-- image -->

## Ankle Sprain Management

## PRICE

- Protection: elastic bandage, splint, walking boot, air cast
- Rest: limit weight bearing until gait normal
- Ice: ice/cold water 15-20 min every 2-3 h ×48 h
- Compression: elastic bandage for support, to minimize swelling. Apply early.
- Elevate: alleviate swelling

## EARLY MOBILITY

- Analgesics: acetaminophen and NSAIDs

## NOTES

## NOTES Gout

- Symptoms: severe pain, redness, warmth, swelling
- $ Onset more often at night
- Presentation and risk factors: Ma'am
- $ Monoarticular: first MTP, knee most common
- $ Atraumatic
- $ Alcohol
- $ Meats and meds (thiazide and loop diuretics, recent use of urate-lowering medications, seafood, liver, red meat)
- Confirmatory diagnostic test:
- $ Synovial fluid analysis

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## QUESTION #9

A patient presents with their third acute gout flare within 12 months. In addition to lifestyle modifications, the best management plan is to prescribe:

1. an anti-inflammatory agent only.
2. allopurinol only.
3. colchicine prophylactically.
4. allopurinol and an anti-inflammatory.

## Gout Treatment

Acute flare: (based on patient characteristics)

- Colchicine (avoid with renal/hepatic impairment)
- NSAIDs (avoid with CVD, GI bleed, renal impairment)
- Glucocorticoids (intra-articular, intramuscular, or oral)

Prophylaxis: urate-lowering therapy

- ≥2 flares annually
- Intolerance to acute medications
- Evidence of tophi or radiographic damage
- Anti-inflammatory prophylaxis: 3-6 months after initiation of urate-lowering therapy
- First-line: allopurinol

- Most are asymptomatic

When in doubt, send it out! (Refer to specialty or order further imaging).
